title: Workflow Automation
description: Chaining, routing, parallelising and orchestrating LLM steps into dependable pipelines.

options.text: Breaking a task into sequential steps where each LLM call uses the previous step's output

questions.explanation: Chaining trades a little latency for accuracy: each step is simpler and you can add checks between steps.

questions.prompt: In a routing workflow, what does the router do?

options.text: Classifies the input and sends it to the most suitable specialised handler

questions.explanation: Routing lets each downstream prompt or model specialise, rather than one prompt trying to handle every case.

questions.prompt: When does running LLM calls in parallel make sense?

options.text: When each step depends on the previous one
When subtasks are independent of each other

questions.explanation: Independent subtasks (for example, checking several documents) can run concurrently to cut latency, then be aggregated.

questions.prompt: In an orchestrator-workers pattern, what does the orchestrator do?

options.text: Dynamically breaks the task into subtasks, delegates them to workers and combines the results

questions.explanation: The orchestrator plans and delegates at run time, which suits tasks where the subtasks are not known in advance.

questions.prompt: Why make each step of an automated workflow idempotent?

options.text: So retries after a failure do not cause duplicate side effects
So it runs faster on the first try
So the model gives creative answers

questions.explanation: Failures and retries are normal. Idempotent steps (for example, keyed by a request id) can be safely re-run without double-charging or double-sending.

options.text: A tool that picks the cheapest model
A model generates output and another call critiques it, iterating until it meets criteria

questions.explanation: One call drafts, another evaluates against clear criteria and gives feedback, and the loop repeats until the bar is met or a limit is reached.
